title: Defining and Calling Functions
objective: Define a function with def and call it with the right number of arguments.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A function is a named block of code you can run again and again without rewriting it. You create one with def, a name, parentheses, and a colon; the indented lines beneath are its body, and they only run when the function is called.

The names inside the parentheses in a def line are parameters — placeholders for values the function needs. When you call the function, the values you provide in its parentheses are arguments, and they get matched to the parameters in order.
Defining a function does not run it. Nothing inside the body executes until the function is called by name, with parentheses, somewhere else in the program.
explanation.rule: def name(parameters): creates a function; name(arguments) is what actually runs it.

examples.title: Define, Then Call
examples.note: Nothing prints until the last line calls strike_anvil with an argument.

checks.question: You write a function with def but never call it anywhere. What happens?
options: It runs automatically at the end of the file.
Python raises an error for an unused function.
Nothing — its body never executes until it's called.
It runs once when Python starts.

feedback.correct: Correct — defining a function only creates it; calling it is what runs the body.
feedback.incorrect: def only creates the function. Its body runs only when the function is called.

assignment.title: Strike the Anvil
assignment.brief: Write strike_anvil(times) that prints the exact text 'Striking ' followed by times followed by ' times.'
requirements: Call strike_anvil(3) so it actually runs.
assignment.starterCode:
def strike_anvil(times):
    # Print 'Striking ' followed by times followed by ' times.'
    pass

strike_anvil(3)
assignment.testHarness:
# ---- Code Forge validation ----
import io, contextlib
_cf_buf = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(_cf_buf):
    strike_anvil(3)
_cf_result = _cf_buf.getvalue()
print("__CF_TEST_OUTPUT__")
print(repr(_cf_result))

hints: Use str(times) to convert the parameter to text before joining it with +.
The parameter times is used directly inside the function body.
Build the full message, then print it in one call.
strike_anvil(3) should print exactly: Striking 3 times.
